This is precisely why homeostasis is the first topic in Module 8: every disease and disorder you study, from cancer to kidney failure to hearing loss, can be traced back to a biological system that has stopped maintaining the internal environment within its tolerance range. The clinician's job is to understand what went wrong and how to restore or replace the homeostatic function that has been lost. he tolerance range is the band either side of it within which the variable is allowed to vary. A stimulus is any change that moves the variable outside that range. Receptors are specialised cells that detect the deviation — thermoreceptors for temperature, osmoreceptors for solute concentration — and they send information to the control centre, usually the hypothalamus, which compares the detected value against the set point and issues a signal. Naming the receptor type and the control centre by name is what turns a generic recital into an interpretation of this particular loop. 4 Read the response direction The effec

eat far more often than ectotherms of similar mass. Ectotherms An ectotherm does not generate meaningful metabolic heat. Its body temperature is determined mainly by the environment, so it rises and falls with the surroundings. Reptiles, amphibians, fish and insects are ectotherms. The benefit is efficiency. An ectotherm needs a fraction of the food an endotherm of the same mass requires, which is one reason reptiles do so well across arid Australia where food supply is unpredictable. Above about 40 °C in humans this becomes dangerous, which is why heat stroke is a medical emergency rather than just discomfort. Cooling causes a different problem. Enzymes and their substrates move more slowly, so they collide less often and reaction rates drop. Nothing is destroyed, but metabolism slows, and below about 35 °C coordination, judgement and heart rhythm are all affected. So homeostasis here is not about hitting one perfect number.
